title: How did a machine to clean cotton expand slavery?
teaches: Upland cotton's sticky seeds and Whitney's saw gin; Indian Removal and the domestic slave trade; climate as the limit and slavery as the labour system; the debate on slavery and industrial capitalism

parts.title: Fifty men with the old machines

blocks.text: On 11 September 1793 Eli Whitney, a 27-year-old Yale graduate who had gone south to take a post as a tutor and stayed instead on a Georgia plantation, wrote to his father in Massachusetts about a machine he had built there for cleaning cotton of its seeds. It was so effective, he wrote, that "one man and a horse will do more than fifty men with the old machines". He patented the **cotton gin** the following year and expected to grow rich from it.

In most of the inventions in this course, a machine made the work easier for the people who did it. The cotton gin did the opposite. In 1790 the United States had about 700,000 enslaved people and grew very little cotton. In 1860 it had almost four million enslaved people, most of them in the cotton states, and grew about two thirds of the world's cotton. In this lesson we look at the problem the gin solved, and at why a machine that saved labour at one step led to a vast increase in forced labour at another.

Lesson 2 described ginning: separating cotton fibre from the seeds it grows on. Indian cotton growers had long used a **roller gin**, the *charkhi* (not to be confused with the *charkha*, the spinning wheel of lesson 21), in which the cotton was fed between two rollers turning against each other; the fibre passed through and the smooth seeds were pushed back. The roller gin worked for the long-staple Sea Island cotton grown on the coast of Georgia and South Carolina, whose black seeds come away cleanly. But Sea Island cotton needs a mild, damp coastal climate and grows only in a narrow strip.

Inland, planters could grow **upland** cotton, a different variety with fibres shorter than Sea Island's and green, fuzzy seeds that the fibre clings to. Roller gins crushed these seeds or let them through, so upland cotton had to be cleaned by hand, and one person could clean only about a pound of fibre a day. British mills (lesson 14) would buy all the cotton they could get, but no farm could clean enough upland cotton to sell it in quantity, so the slow cleaning step kept it from becoming a large cash crop.

Whitney's **saw gin** pulled the fibre off instead of squeezing it through. A cylinder set with rows of wire teeth, later replaced by toothed saw blades, turned against a grid of bars spaced too narrowly for seeds to pass. The teeth caught the fibre and pulled it through the gaps; the seeds stayed behind, and a brush cleared the teeth. It was simple enough for local blacksmiths and carpenters to copy, and many did. Whitney and his business partner, Phineas Miller, spent years suing copiers and made little money from it.

Climate set where upland cotton could be grown. It needs about 200 days a year without frost, a hot summer, enough rain while growing and dry weather at harvest. Much of the American South met those conditions. Who would grow it, and on whose land, was decided by law and force.

blocks.text: Much of the best cotton land in 1800 belonged to Native nations: the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole. Through wars, forced treaties and, after the **Indian Removal Act** of 1830, deportation, the federal government took that land and moved its peoples west of the Mississippi. Several thousand Cherokee died on the forced march of 1838 and 1839, and thousands more from other nations on similar marches, which the Cherokee remember as the Trail of Tears. The land, tens of millions of acres in Alabama, Mississippi, Georgia and beyond, was surveyed and sold, much of it to planters for cotton.

The labour came from slavery. Congress banned the import of enslaved Africans from 1808, so planters in the new cotton states bought people from the older slave states of Virginia and Maryland, where tobacco farming needed fewer workers. Between 1790 and 1860 about a million enslaved people were moved from the upper South (Virginia, Maryland, Kentucky and their neighbours) to the lower South (from Georgia west to Louisiana and Texas), many of them sold away from their families and marched overland in chained lines called coffles. Slave prices rose and fell with the price of cotton.

blocks.text: The gin removed the bottleneck in cleaning, which was the only step a machine could easily do. Planting, hoeing, thinning and above all picking stayed by hand, and the more cotton the gin could clean, the more hands were wanted in the fields. A machine that saved labour at one step multiplied the demand for forced labour at the others. Picking rates per enslaved worker rose several times between 1800 and 1860; historians disagree about how much of that came from violence and how much from better seed varieties, which is part of the larger debate below.

parts.title: Historians disagree: slavery and industrial capitalism

blocks.text: How much did slavery contribute to industrialisation in Britain and the United States? **Eric Williams**, in *Capitalism and Slavery* (1944), argued that the profits of the slave trade and the Caribbean plantations helped finance British industry. **Stanley Engerman** and **Patrick O'Brien** later estimated those profits and found them small compared with total British investment, too small to be decisive. **Joseph Inikori**, whom lesson 13 introduced, argued that the measure should be the markets slavery created, not only its profits.

A second round of debate followed in the 2010s. **Sven Beckert**, in *Empire of Cotton* (2014), described the cotton economy as built on what he called war capitalism: land taken by force and labour coerced by slavery, organised by merchants and states. **Edward Baptist**, in *The Half Has Never Been Told* (2014), argued that rising picking rates came from systematic torture and that slavery made up a large share of the American economy. Economic historians including **Alan Olmstead** and **Paul Rhode** responded that Baptist's figures double-counted economic activity, and that most of the rise in picking rates came from new cotton varieties with larger bolls that were easier to pick. They do not dispute the violence of slavery, which is documented in detail; they dispute how much it explains of the growth in output.

These debates turn on numbers that are hard to measure, and on what counts as a contribution. Two points are not in dispute. By the 1850s, about three quarters of the raw cotton used in British mills came from the American South. And that cotton was grown on land taken from Native nations and picked by enslaved people, whose numbers grew with every expansion of the crop.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the gin and the cotton South.

items.ask: Indian roller gins had worked for centuries. Why were they no use for upland cotton?
choices: Its fuzzy seeds cling, so rollers crush them
Rollers were too expensive to make in America
Upland cotton has no seeds for rollers to remove
Roller gins needed water power the uplands lacked
items.why: Rollers work for smooth-seeded cottons. Upland cotton's seeds hold the fibre tightly, which Whitney's teeth solved by pulling the fibre off.

items.ask: The gin made cleaning cotton far faster. Why did the demand for enslaved labour rise rather than fall?
choices: Planters grew far more, and picking stayed by hand
Each gin needed dozens of people to keep it running
Enslaved people were needed to build the new gins
Cotton prices rose so high that every farm grew it
items.why: A machine at one step removed a bottleneck. Output grew until the hand steps, picking above all, needed many more workers.

items.ask: Cotton spread across a huge area of the South between 1800 and 1860. What decided who got that land?
choices: Wars, treaties and Native removal, then land sales
The climate alone, since cotton grew wherever it was warm
British cotton firms, which bought the land directly
The first planters to arrive, who claimed land freely
items.why: Climate made the land suitable; law and force decided who owned it and who worked it.

items.ask: Congress banned the import of enslaved people from 1808. How did the cotton states get workers after that?
choices: By buying people from the older slave states
By hiring free workers who came from Europe
By smuggling captives in despite the ban
By using new machines to pick the cotton
items.why: The domestic slave trade moved people from Virginia and Maryland to the cotton states, often separating families.

items.ask: Olmstead and Rhode disagree with Baptist about rising picking rates. What do they argue?
choices: New varieties with larger bolls explain most of it
Slavery in the cotton fields was not violent
Picking rates did not rise at all before 1860
Machines did much of the picking by the 1850s
items.why: Their dispute is about the cause of the productivity gain, not about the brutality of slavery, which both sides document.

summary: **Upland cotton had a cleaning bottleneck.** Its fuzzy seeds cling to the fibre, and roller gins could not separate them.
**Whitney's saw gin solved it.** From 1793, teeth pulled the fibre through bars too narrow for seeds; copies spread fast.
**Climate set the limit.** Upland cotton needs about 200 frost-free days, which much of the South had.
**Force decided who had the land.** Removal of Native nations, especially after 1830, opened tens of millions of acres to planters.
**Slavery supplied the labour.** The enslaved population grew from about 700,000 in 1790 to almost four million in 1860.
**A domestic slave trade moved people south.** About a million were taken from the upper South to the cotton states.
**The fix multiplied forced labour.** The gin sped one step, and the hand steps, picking above all, needed far more people.
**Historians disagree on how much slavery built industry.** Williams, Engerman and O'Brien, Inikori, Beckert, Baptist, and Olmstead and Rhode weigh profits, markets and productivity differently.
**The American South supplied Britain's mills.** By the 1850s about three quarters of the cotton spun in Lancashire came from it.
